articles.title: 3D DRAM created by IBM and Micron, 128GBps memory on the way
articles.summary: Smaller and faster RAM with up to 128GB transfer speed scould be on the way thanks to research from IBM and MIcron, using stacked chips and TSVs.
articles.body: Smaller and faster RAM with up to 128GBps transfer speeds could be on the way thanks to research from IBM and MIcron. The companies have developed three-dimensional memory, stacking individual DRAM chips vertically that would normally have to be placed side-by-side, though the efficiencies gained aren’t solely down to space. Communication between the stacked chips and the host device is achieved through a new creation known as through-silicon vias, or TSVs, which run vertically through the pile of chips and act as conduits to the host device. Thanks to the TSVs, in testing the memory has reached data speeds of 128GBps, ten times faster than current memory. On top of this, IBM claims the chips are 70 percent more power efficient than today’s DRAM. The new research is expected to form a key part of Samsung and Micron’s Hybrid Memory Cube technology, first announced back in October. IBM and Micron hope to have commercial availability in two years, with servers likely to use it first. Looking beyond that, IBM fellow Subu Iyer said that the new process “will have applications beyond memory, enabling other industry segments as well.” What exactly those new segments are remains to be seen, but we certainly wouldn’t complain if our computers got the kind of speed bump described here.

articles.title: The Moto Tag is an AirTag for Android
articles.summary: Motorola is introducing a new tracker called the Moto Tag that is compatible with Google’s Find My Device network and has UWB. It’s basically an AirTag, but for Android.
articles.body: Motorola’s tracking tag is officially here, and if you’ve wanted an AirTag for your Android phone, this new Moto Tag might be it. This item tracker costs $29 and works with Google’s newly upgraded Find My Device network to help you locate a lost item. In addition to Bluetooth, it also offers ultra wideband, which means that if your phone is equipped with a UWB chip — like the Samsung Galaxy S24 Ultra — you can track down the tag’s precise location. You know, just like you can with an AirTag. The Moto Tag comes with an IP67 rating, so it should survive a dunk in fresh water. The tag is powered by a CR2032 coin cell battery and should last a full year before it needs a new one. And in the event that you have your tag on hand but can’t find your phone, pressing a button on the Moto Tag will ring your phone to help you find it. The multifunction button can also be used as a remote shutter for your Motorola phone’s camera. [Image: Moto Tags will probably fit in third-party AirTag cases. It also seems that the Moto Tag will work with cases designed to hold an AirTag; according to Motorola’s press release, the tag was “designed specifically to fit perfectly with most third-party accessories already on the market so that users can easily attach it to all their valuables.” There you go — AirTag, but make it Android. The Moto Tag will go on sale on August 2nd; you can buy one for $29 or a four-pack for $99.

articles.title: The Pixel Tag is Google’s answer to the AirTag
articles.summary: The $29 tracker combines UWB with Bluetooth channel sounding.
articles.body: More than two years after launching its own device-tracking network, Google has finally followed up with its own tracker. The Pixel Tag, which goes on sale in November, looks like one of the more capable trackers too: It combines ultra wideband (UWB) with Bluetooth 6.0 Channel Sounding for two distinct types of precision tracking. The Pixel Tag goes on sale on November 11th, unlike the newly announced Pixel 11 and Pixel Watch 5, which are already available to preorder and ship next week. When it arrives, the Tag will cost $29, with a four-pack for $99 — the exact same pricing as Apple’s AirTag 2. The Pixel Tag is a slim oblong device available in one grayish color — Fog — that weighs about 12g, or 0.4oz. Like the AirTag, it has no built-in hooks or clips for attaching to objects you want to track. There’s a single button that will trigger a sound on your phone, for the rare occasion when you’ve got the Tag but have lost your main device. It also has an IP67 rating, so it should be safe from dust and rain. As for the battery, the Pixel Tag takes CR2032 coin batteries, and says one battery should last for over a year. [Image: It only comes in one color, so I hope you like gray — sorry, Fog. Naturally, it’ll be compatible with Google’s Find Hub network, which leverages the Bluetooth capabilities of Android devices worldwide to help locate lost objects. After a rocky launch, the network has improved steadily since, though when I tested it last year I found it was still less precise than Apple’s. Once you’re close enough to the Pixel Tag, UWB lets the Find Hub app display the distance and direction to the tracker, so long as you’re using a phone with a UWB chip. Channel Sounding is a newer development that can display the exact distance, but not direction, and it will work with any phone or tablet that includes Bluetooth 6.0. The Moto Tag 2 is the only other tracker to currently support it. Google device owners will need a Pixel 10 or later to take advantage of Channel Sounding, and any Pro model since the 6 for UWB — even in the new Pixel 11 series, the base model still lacks UWB. You can track the Tag using a Pixel Watch too, and any model since the 4 will support Channel Sounding, while the 2 or later include UWB. You can also ask Gemini to ring the Tag’s speaker for you.

articles.title: Steve Kornacki explains 'abrupt ending' to epic midterm marathon stream
articles.summary: Steve Kornacki is explaining why he dipped out of his marathon midterms stream without saying goodbye: "Things caught up to me in a hurry at hour 10."
articles.body:
Steve Kornacki is back to give viewers some closure after his epic midterms marathon.

The network's chief data analyst went live for a whopping 10 straight hours for NBC News' coverage of the midterm elections Nov. 3. Throughout the evening, Kornacki regularly appeared on the NBC television network to discuss the election results as they came in. But NBC also hosted a " Kornacki Cam " livestream that stayed with Kornacki all night long.

The stream ended a bit abruptly, though: After impressively staying on for more than 10 hours with virtually no breaks, Kornacki told viewers he'd be taking five minutes and would be "right back," only to never return.

In an early morning X post on Nov. 4 , Kornacki explained he had planned to be live for 13 hours but had to dip out a bit earlier than anticipated.

"I was sure 13 hours would be fine but things caught up to me in a hurry at hour 10," he wrote. "I can't say thanks enough to all of you. What a ride and I think we did make livestream history. Sorry for the abrupt ending!"

Prior to Kornacki's update, viewers had joked about the lack of closure to the stream: "I didn't want him to go without saying goodbye," one person wrote in the YouTube comments, while another quipped, "I'm not going to bed until there is proof of life from Steve."

At the start of Kornacki's coverage, which officially kicked off about 30 minutes before the first polls closed, the elections guru told viewers he was embarking on a "grand livestream experiment." All night, the stream would show Kornacki whenever he joined the NBC network for analysis. But in between those segments, the stream would keep on rolling continuously, so Kornacki would continue talking to viewers and providing insights.

"We're doing something we've never done before," he said, explaining, "I'm going to be going into the NBC broadcast. You'll see that on this livestream. I'm going to be coming back when I'm not on NBC, and we're going to be doing results, results, results. We're going to do it all night."

NBC previously utilized the "Kornacki Cam" numerous times during primary election coverage, though prior streams were typically not as lengthy or elaborate as the midterm marathon. "This started as an experiment with a House special election last year and turned into this," Kornacki wrote on X .

In March, Kornacki told The Hollywood Reporter that his "Kornacki Cam" streams allow him to provide the viewer with "a much more kind of comprehensive picture of how the election was won or lost."

Kornacki noted at the start that he was skeptical of how it would work to do a stream in the same studio where NBC anchors Savannah Guthrie and Tom Llamas would be hosting the network's regular election coverage.

"When they told me they wanted to try this, I was like, 'Well, Savannah and Tom are going to want to kill me because I'm going to drive them crazy,'" he said. "But we tested the sound and everything. They said they don't really hear me. I don't really hear them."

Kornacki, famed for providing incisive election analysis and breaking down results by county while standing in front of a screen dubbed the Big Board, also said early on that his plan was to keep streaming "through the morning."

As the stream continued, viewers in the live chat and on social media marveled at Kornacki's stamina, especially considering he was standing the entire time and was rarely off camera for more than a few moments. Even when he wasn't speaking, the feed would usually still show Kornacki looking at his phone or a nearby monitor.

"Steve's multitasking skills is legendary," one viewer commented in the live chat, and YouTuber David Doel praised the stream as possibly the "greatest thing NBC has ever concocted."

At one point, after nine hours of coverage, NBC anchor Craig Melvin addressed viewers who might be confused about how Kornacki was still going. "For those of you who might be concerned about Steve Kornacki's well-being … I can confirm that Steve Kornacki has had a bathroom break, and we are nourishing him, as well."

According to NBC, the "Kornacki Cam" stream was the No. 1 election live stream on YouTube for the midterms, and it amassed 29 million views across platforms.

articles.title: Google derruba esquema que controlava 1 milhão de aparelhos infectados; Brasil é o 2º mais afetado | G1
articles.standfirst: Segundo a empresa, fabricante chinesa instalava programa malicioso de fábrica e vendia acesso aos dispositivos para criminosos. Maioria dos equipamentos era de TV boxes com Android.
articles.summary: Segundo a empresa, fabricante chinesa instalava programa malicioso de fábrica e vendia acesso aos dispositivos para criminosos. Maioria dos equipamentos era de TV boxes com Android.
articles.body:
Google derruba rede com 1,3 milhão de aparelhos infectados, incluindo TV boxes; Brasil é o 2º mais afetado — Foto: Reprodução/Google

Uma operação do Google com outras empresas de tecnologia desmantelou uma rede que controlava mais de 1,3 milhão de aparelhos sem o conhecimento dos donos. Os dispositivos tinham um programa malicioso chamado XCPE, instalado de fábrica. A maioria era de TV boxes com Android .

O Brasil foi o segundo país com mais dispositivos afetados , atrás apenas da Malásia, segundo a empresa de cibersegurança Trend Micro. Foram identificados aparelhos infectados em 170 países. Iraque, México e Taiwan também estão entre os mais atingidos.

Segundo o Google, a fabricante Videostrong, sediada em Shenzhen, na China, instalou intencionalmente o programa no sistema dos equipamentos. A infecção não dependia de o usuário clicar em um link suspeito: os aparelhos já saíam de fábrica com o vírus.

A fabricante ganhava dinheiro vendendo a criminosos o acesso aos aparelhos infectados . Eles usavam os dispositivos para simular visualizações de anúncios e gerar receita com publicidade.

Embora a maioria dos aparelhos infectados fosse de TV boxes, o Google também identificou o programa em dispositivos de telemedicina, máquinas de karaokê e equipamentos de sinalização digital.

Fabricantes podem firmar contratos com o Google para oferecer serviços da empresa em seus aparelhos, como o Android TV. Segundo o Google, essas empresas precisam cumprir requisitos e passar por testes de compatibilidade e segurança.

A Videostrong, porém, usou técnicas para esconder o programa e burlar essas verificações, afirmou o Google. Isso permitia carregar código malicioso após o aparelho ser ligado pela primeira vez .

Segundo a empresa, a Videostrong adotava essa prática desde o fim de 2024.

"Um fabricante de dispositivos infectar intencionalmente seus usuários com malware é uma quebra inaceitável de confiança e representa um risco sério para esses usuários", disse o Google.

A empresa informou que rompeu relações com a Videostrong e proibiu ela de produzir e vender aparelhos Android certificados ou fornecer software a outros fabricantes certificados. Também afirmou que alterou seu processo de revisão para proteger os consumidores.

Aparelho de TV Box da Videostrong — Foto: Reprodução/Videostrong

Procurada pelo g1 , a Agência Nacional de Telecomunicações (Anatel) afirmou que combate a venda de produtos não homologados devido aos riscos para os consumidores e para as redes de telecomunicações.

"O impacto da utilização de equipamentos não homologados vai muito além das questões de qualidade do serviço fornecido ao consumidor ou da segurança física do aparelho. Trata-se de uma ameaça direta à infraestrutura cibernética do país", afirmou ao g1 Gesiléa Fonseca Teles, superintendente de fiscalização da agência.

"A proteção das telecomunicações exige vigilância constante, cooperação institucional e a conscientização de que a integridade da rede depende da procedência e conformidade do hardware conectado", completou.

A Anatel não participou da operação. Segundo o Google, a ação envolveu a Agência Nacional de Polícia do Japão e as empresas Lumen, HUMAN Security, Plume, Synthient e TrendAI.

articles.body: Television actress Indira Krishna, who will be seen in Bollywood's mythological saga Ramayana as Mata Kaushalya, recalled her first day with the Ramayana cast. She took a trip down memory lane and recalled the first day of the cast reading session for Nitesh Tiwari's much-anticipated film 'Ramayana', featuring Ranbir Kapoor and Sai Pallavi in the lead roles.She took to her social media account to share a series of pictures from the memorable day. Indira expressed nostalgia and penned heartfelt notes for her co-stars and the film's team. She praised Ranbir Kapoor with whom she has shared screen space in two films, 'Animal' and 'Ramayana'.Praising Ranbir, she said she witnessed the actor's journey from 'Animal' to 'Ramayana' and described him as a beautiful person both inside and out. She also lauded his performance and said he nailed his role.Sharing her memories, Indira wrote, "Our first day of cast reading session. What a memorable day and today I could feel this nostalgia. RK I hv no words to tell how beautiful inside out u are. From Animal to Ramayana I witnessed this pure soul actor and believe me he nailed it. Take a bow RK."Talking about Sai Pallavi, who plays Goddess Sita, Indira praised her innocence and spiritual thoughts. She added that their coming together for the film seemed destined. She also expressed gratitude towards Ravi for looking after her during their time in Chandigarh and described him as a sweetheart.She added, “Sai ur innocence speaks volumes and ur spiritual thought has brought u to this platform ..ur right we all were destined to meet here.”She went on to praise director Nitesh Tiwari and said she was impressed by the way he guided the cast to bring out the emotions in their performances. She recalled a particular scene before the Vanvas sequence and shared she still remembered how the filmmaker helped her get the shot right in one take.She further praised Rakul Preet Singh for her politeness and cheerful nature and appreciated her portrayal of Surpanakha. Indira went on to thank casting director Mukesh Chhabra for knowing the right cast from the very beginning. She also acknowledged Jay Kar's work and recalled experiencing an elaborate camera setup involving more than 80 cameras.While concluding her note, the actress expressed love and gratitude to the entire team and wrote, "Love u all ..cheers to the team cheers to Namit Malhotra's Ramayana..JAI SHREE RAM."Indira Krishnan plays Mata Kaushalya, the mother of Lord Ram (played by Ranbir Kapoor), in Nitesh Tiwari's 'Ramayana.’'Ramayana' is slated to hit theatres today, November 5, 2026, across India.Get the latest TV News, TV Shows and more. articles.title: Where is Windows 12?
articles.summary: Microsoft seems happy to stick with Windows 11, for now.﻿
articles.body: While I wasn’t expecting Microsoft to announce Windows 12 during its RTX Spark launch event last month, more than a few people were hoping to see something truly new. Between the growing frustration with Windows 11 and the muted response to Copilot Plus PCs, it’s starting to feel like Microsoft needs to go bigger with its desktop OS. Much of this year’s Windows development has been focused on underlying performance improvements, after Microsoft acknowledged the bloat and reliability issues with Windows 11 and created a plan to fix them. That work is ongoing, and sources tell me there’s now a big focus on quality for the next major release of Windows 11 in 2027. Microsoft started planning to shift back to a three-year release cycle for Windows in 2022, with the first big release in 2024. At the time, many expected that to be Windows 12, but the company stuck to a major update of Windows 11 instead. Now that the three-year cycle is about to hit again, it looks like Microsoft is promising to improve Windows 11 instead of rolling new features and underlying improvements into a Windows 12 release. Sources tell me that Microsoft is already preparing for Windows 11 version 27H2. Like the big 24H2 release in 2024, this will be a full OS swap, where Microsoft replaces or upgrades major parts of the OS. The past couple of annual releases (25H2 and 26H2) have been enablement packages, which simply switch new features on gradually as they’re rolled out in monthly cumulative updates. Since this is a bigger release, more testing will be required for the new features and changes that Microsoft is planning to make next year. We will likely see Windows Insider testing begin a lot sooner than the typical June timeframe Microsoft used for both 25H2 and 26H2. Microsoft is also preparing for the big release of Windows 11 next year by replacing the default wallpaper of the operating system. Sources tell me a new wallpaper will be unveiled at Microsoft’s Ignite conference later this month, with a series of designs replacing Bloom, the current default. Microsoft used Bloom to market Windows 11 heavily during its launch phase, with “Bloomberry” ice cream and the wallpaper gracing the famous Times Square screens. [Image: One of the new Windows 11 wallpapers. The wallpaper replacements will vary across consumer and commercial versions of Windows 11, I’m told. The designs are similar to Bloom, but with a folding sheet of color immersed in clouds. The Windows 11 Pro version looks the most like the Bloom colors, while there are subtle variations for the consumer versions of Windows 11, focused on gaming, productivity, creator, and performance. Microsoft has quietly started using some of these new wallpapers in its recent Windows 11 marketing materials, and it plans to preview the full Bloom replacement at Ignite before rolling it out broadly in early January. The question I can’t answer yet is whether Microsoft will even consider moving to Windows 12 branding next year, or whether that’s still a few years away. Microsoft seems to be set on improving Windows 11’s reputation, but it’s a difficult task to achieve when lots of people have already made their minds up. Even Microsoft’s performance improvements haven’t convinced everyone yet. Microsoft showed off some more of its memory optimization work earlier this week, improving performance and multitasking on PCs with 8GB of RAM. “Windows can now keep up to 2 GB more of your active data in memory instead of moving it to slower storage, so an app or tab you left open is less likely to reload when you return,” explains Windows chief Pavan Davuluri. I’ve seen YouTubers and even some Windows Insiders question this work, skeptical that Microsoft is actually making improvements. But it’s not just a false promise from Windows engineers; there’s a big effort to make a series of small improvements that all add up to a better performance across a variety of hardware. Windows Central tested Microsoft’s claims and found that the latest updates to Windows 11 do, in fact, improve memory usage. Paging less data to disk will also improve performance, particularly when you’re multitasking between apps on a system with just 8GB of RAM. Microsoft is making improvements to memory usage in apps like Word, PowerPoint, Excel, and Outlook, too, so this isn’t even just a Windows effort anymore. These changes are hard to notice unless you compare two systems side by side, and Microsoft clearly has a perception problem with Windows 11 that steady improvements like this won’t overcome. Microsoft ultimately missed a chance to simply own up to the malware-like ads it has squeezed into Windows 11 and be transparent about the fact that they were a mistake. Instead, I think the company is betting that it can win back users over the long term through genuine improvements rather than a marketing exercise that packages everything up into a shiny, new Windows 12 release. Whether that’s enough to change how people feel about Windows remains to be seen, but Microsoft needs to give people a reason to be excited about Windows again, not just another reason to tolerate it. The pad * The biggest names in AI are backing a new way to opt out of scraping. OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, and Anthropic are all promising to adopt a new standard that will allow publishers to opt out of being scraped by AI bots. As Google Zero continues to reshape the publishing industry, Microsoft says websites will still appear in Bing’s search results even if AI training has been blocked. Anthropic has already adopted this new signal, which is part of a website’s robots.txt file, and Google and Microsoft are both planning to support it next year. * Curry Barker used a Surface Laptop Ultra to help make his new YouTube short. Microsoft is promoting the performance benefits of RTX Spark on battery by showcasing that Obsession director Curry Barker used a Surface Laptop Ultra to edit the full Mama Bear film while unplugged. The edit obviously wasn’t performed on a single battery charge, as Microsoft notes, but it’s more to point out that Windows laptops have finally caught up to the MacBook Pro’s ability to maintain near-identical performance whether on battery or plugged in. * Windows 11 tries new shortcuts for Xbox gaming mode and search. Microsoft has started testing new Windows 11 builds that improve on the recently refreshed Windows Search and add quick settings to Xbox mode. Windows Insiders can now test out filters in search for files, actions, or web results, as well as perform actions like changing screen brightness or volume. The Xbox mode in Windows 11 is also getting quick settings to easily toggle things like Bluetooth and Wi-Fi without having to exit to the desktop mode on a handheld gaming PC. * Xbox’s former COO has “serious concerns” about her abrupt departure. I said this was weird last week. Xbox’s former chief operating officer, Helen Chiang, suddenly left Microsoft less than two weeks ago after being promoted into the role in July. A surprisingly short memo from Xbox CEO Asha Sharma revealed the news internally, and now Chiang says she has “serious concerns” about how she was treated. In a lengthy post on LinkedIn, Chiang doesn’t dispute she was fired but says a Eurogamer report that it was related to policy violations is “not accurate.” Chiang also denies unfounded rumors that speculated she was leaking information, or that she left to join a competitor. I’ve only heard really positive things about Chiang, so this whole turn of events is very puzzling. * The Elder Scrolls VI officially has a name: Sentinel. I reported in Notepad last week that Sentinel would be the official subtitle of The Elder Scrolls VI, and Bethesda confirmed it this week with a brief teaser video. While the game is still at least two years away from release, Bethesda has been showing off some parts of the story internally in recent months. There have been many leaks about The Elder Scrolls VI in recent years, and I will say that one was very accurate, while many others have been far off the mark. * Xbox’s smallest-ever controller is surprisingly comfortable. I’ve been testing out the new $49.99 Xbox Nano controller over the past few days, and I’m impressed with the design. I have small hands so it’s perfectly suited to me, and it’s designed for younger people and gaming on the go. The big difference with the Nano over regular Xbox controllers is the size of the triggers. They’re also a lot more clicky than the thud on the regular controller. The battery life is also something you’ll have to get used to, as it seems to drain fully in around five to six hours. * Xbox’s Arkane Studios attracts multiple bidders, including Ubisoft. We’re just weeks away from hearing about the fate of Blade developers Arkane Studios, and it looks like Microsoft has some options lined up for the studio. Bloomberg reports that Ubisoft and “at least two other gaming companies” have made bids for Arkane. Microsoft is also considering selling the studio to its management. I wrote last week that “I’m cautiously optimistic that Blade will be saved.” * Microsoft is improving Outlook search with a small language model. Microsoft has heard the feedback about Outlook search and it’s looking to improve result ranking, results when connectivity is poor, and a better feedback loop for end users. Classic Outlook will now automatically fall back to a local index when connectivity to cloud servers is poor. This should improve the speed of results, but Microsoft is also using an Outlook-specific small language model ranker to improve the relevancy and speed of results. You’ll also be able to use a thumbs up or down on Outlook search results to let Microsoft know how happy you are with the changes. * The new Windows 11 speed test was built by an AI agent. Microsoft saw the feedback about the taskbar speed test throwing you to a webpage, and it designed a fully integrated version for Windows 11 instead. “The design and build work was driven by an agentic AI workflow, with a person guiding the process in their spare time,” says Marcus Ash, head of design and research for Windows and devices. It took only a day to get a working prototype ready. “This is where I see a lot of potential in AI,” says Ash. “Getting from idea to customer value faster. Without AI slop. That is the way.” * Xbox previews two new ways to control cloud games. Microsoft’s new Xbox Nano controller now supports a Wi-Fi connection directly to Xbox Cloud Gaming, just like Google’s Stadia controllers. It was a hidden feature when I tried out the new controller recently, and US players will be able to preview it ahead of a broader rollout. Microsoft is also previewing a new phone controller option for playing cloud games on smart TVs. * Xbox overhauls its PC, web, and cloud apps with a faster design. Microsoft is unveiling a new Xbox PC app today that launches “up to 60 percent faster” than before, with an overhauled design to match new updates to Xbox Cloud Gaming on the web and smart TVs. Xbox Insiders will be able to start testing the updated Xbox PC app today, and the updated Xbox Cloud Gaming interface will start rolling out over the next few weeks. I’ve been trying out the new Xbox PC app on the Xbox Ally X handheld in recent weeks, and it’s noticeably faster and feels much more like I’m navigating an Xbox console interface than before. It’s good to see these much-needed improvements for the Xbox PC app. I’m always keen to hear from readers, so please drop a comment here, or you can reach me at notepad@theverge.com if you want to discuss anything else. If you’ve heard about any of Microsoft’s secret projects, you can reach me via email at notepad@theverge.com or speak to me confidentially on the Signal messaging app, where I’m tomwarren.01. I’m also tomwarren on Telegram, if you’d prefer to chat there. Thanks for subscribing to Notepad.

articles.title: Ember’s smallest self-heating mug is on sale for just $33
articles.summary: The six-ounce Ember Cup is on sale for $32.99 ($67 off) at Woot until November 8th, making it a more affordable alternative to the company’s pricier smart mugs.
articles.body: We’ve been fans of Ember’s temperature-controlled mugs for years, though given the price tag, we admit that they’re somewhat of a luxury purchase. Thankfully, if you’ve been looking for a more affordable option, Woot is selling the Ember Cup in black for $32.99 ($67 off) with a 90-day warranty through November 7th. You can potentially save even more as part of Woot’s larger Home and Kitchen Sale, which lets you save an additional $20 off orders of $100 or more when you use code COOK at checkout. [Product: Ember Cup (six-ounce) | Granted, six ounces isn’t much, but the smaller, handle-free cup is well-suited for cappuccinos, cortados, flat whites, and other espresso-based drinks. It’s also a perfectly fine option if you don’t mind refilling your cup of coffee, cocoa, or tea throughout the day. I’m actually tempted to pick one up myself at this price, especially since I’ve been trying (with varying degrees of success) to cut back on coffee. Like Ember’s larger mugs, the smart cup lets you choose and set your drinking temperature between 120 and 145 degrees Fahrenheit using a companion app, then remembers your setting for future drinks. It can then maintain that temperature for up to 95 minutes on a charge, up to four hours with a lid, or even all day if you leave it on the included charging dock. The cup also automatically enters sleep mode after two hours of inactivity to conserve power. Just keep in mind that, despite its IPX7 water-resistance rating, the cup is hand-wash only.

articles.body: Android fans with a bit of iPhone Duo envy, take note: The Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 is discounted to $1,599.99 at both Amazon and Best Buy, a hefty $300 markdown from its usual price, and just $50 higher than the lowest we’ve seen. Considering the device only launched a few months ago, you’re saving a significant amount of cash on the unlocked device, and you can also opt for the 512GB model, doubling the storage, for just $200 more (Amazon, Best Buy). Best Buy currently has all three colors in stock, while the 256GB model is currently sold out on Amazon in cream. [Product: Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 | The shorter and wider passport-style shape (similar to the iPhone Duo) quickly became natural and comfortable to handle, according to our reviewer Dominic Preston’s experience with the Z Fold 8. Despite its thin and light construction, it doesn’t skimp on battery life, with a 4,800mAh battery that still had 40 percent charge remaining after a full day of use. The interior 4:3 screen has the same ratio as most Apple iPads, which is great for watching movies or TV, but even better for reading. There’s no telephoto lens on this model (it’s present on the pricier Z Fold 8 Ultra), and it only has an IP48 rating, so you’ll want to be careful near the beach, but those are small compromises to make given the discounted price. Read our Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 review. Other deals to consider * Both Amazon and Best Buy are selling the Beats Pill for a discounted $99.95 and $99.99 respectively, a sizable break from the usual $149.99 price point. The 2024 edition of this iconic Bluetooth speaker adds in lossless audio over USB-C, as well as native feature support for both iOS and Android devices. It’s rated IP67 for dust and water resistance, and comes in three different colors to match your other Beats devices. Read our review. * The Ring Battery Doorbell 2K is on sale for $39.99 at Amazon, over half off its $99.99 list price. This battery-powered doorbell camera is easy to install, and shoots clear 2K resolution video with a 140-degree field of view and up to 6X digital zoom. You’ll get real-time notifications on your phone for any activity the camera spots, with live view and two-way talk in case you need to have a chat with your neighbors or delivery folks without coming to the front door. * You can pick up the Lego Star Wars: Ahsoka Chopper set for just $66.99 at Amazon, the lowest price we’ve seen yet for this 1,039-piece building kit. This brick-based droid has great play features, like detachable arms and center wheel for different display positions, and a head that spins and bobs realistically. It stands at over 8.5 inches when fully built, making it a fun addition to your existing Lego display or bookshelf.

articles.title: DTV+, SmartBox e TV Stick: entenda as diferenças e funções de cada um | G1
articles.standfirst: Apesar de ampliarem as possibilidades da televisão, equipamentos têm funções diferentes e atendem a necessidades específicas do consumidor
articles.summary: Apesar de ampliarem as possibilidades da televisão, equipamentos têm funções diferentes e atendem a necessidades específicas do consumidor
articles.body:
Com diferentes equipamentos disponíveis para ampliar as funções da televisão, é comum surgir a dúvida sobre qual solução escolher. Receptor DTV+, SmartBox e TV Stick podem até parecer semelhantes, mas cada um tem uma finalidade e recursos próprios.

Receptor DTV+: acesso à nova geração da TV aberta

Tela de televisão apresenta interface de aplicativos e canais da TV aberta. — Foto: Divulgação

O receptor DTV+ está diretamente ligado à chegada da TV 3.0, nova geração da televisão aberta. A tecnologia permite que televisores compatíveis recebam o novo padrão de transmissão sem que o consumidor precise trocar o aparelho.

Uma das opções disponíveis no mercado é o KIT DTV+ Antena e Receptor MIMO (PRODTV-1000), da Proeletronic, que reúne receptor e antena para a recepção do novo sinal.

O receptor é compatível com imagens de até 4K Ultra HD e HDR10 e conta com suporte ao áudio MPEG-H, associado à experiência de som imersivo da TV 3.0. O equipamento também possui Android embarcado, Wi-Fi Dual Band, Bluetooth 5.0 e conexão Ethernet.

A solução conta ainda com dupla entrada de antena, contribuindo para a recepção de sinais de alta resolução. A escolha entre antena interna ou externa depende das condições de recepção de cada local.

A conexão com a internet amplia as possibilidades da TV 3.0, como recursos de interatividade e acesso a conteúdos complementares. A programação da televisão aberta, no entanto, continua sendo recebida pelo sinal terrestre.

SmartBox: mais recursos para televisores convencionais

SmartBox conectada à televisão oferece acesso a aplicativos, plataformas de streaming e conteúdos pela internet. — Foto: Divulgação

Já a SmartBox tem outra proposta. O equipamento permite transformar uma televisão convencional em SmartTV, com acesso a aplicativos, plataformas de streaming, jogos e outros conteúdos pela internet.

O SmartPRO 4K HD (PROSB-3000/16GB), da Proeletronic, utiliza Android 10 e conta com acesso à Google Play Store, 2 GB de memória RAM e 16 GB de armazenamento interno.

O modelo também possui conexões HDMI e A/V, permitindo o uso em diferentes modelos de televisão, além de duas portas USB e entrada para cartão SD. A SmartBox também permite reproduzir vídeos, músicas e fotos, além de acessar os aplicativos disponíveis na plataforma.

TV Stick permite acessar aplicativos e plataformas de streaming diretamente na televisão. — Foto: Divulgação

O TV Stick também leva recursos de uma Smart TV para televisores convencionais, mas tem um formato mais compacto. O dispositivo é conectado diretamente à entrada HDMI do televisor.

O StickPRO 4K HD (PROSK-1000), da Proeletronic, utiliza Android 10, tem acesso à Google Play Store, Wi-Fi Dual Band, Bluetooth 5.0 e suporta resolução de até 4K. O dispositivo também conta com controle remoto com comando de voz, que permite pesquisar conteúdos, acessar aplicativos e navegar pelas funções da televisão de forma mais prática.

Por ser conectado diretamente à entrada HDMI, o TV Stick ocupa menos espaço. O modelo também conta com entrada USB e suporte a cartão Micro SD, que permitem acessar conteúdos compatíveis, como vídeos, fotos e músicas.

Assim como a Smart Box, o TV Stick utiliza a internet para acessar aplicativos e plataformas de streaming. A principal diferença está no formato e na forma de conexão com a televisão.

Embora os três equipamentos ampliem as possibilidades de uso da televisão, suas funções são diferentes. O receptor DTV+ está voltado para a recepção da nova geração da TV aberta, enquanto SmartBox e TV Stick permitem levar recursos de SmartTV e acesso a aplicativos para televisores que não possuem essas funções integradas.

“É importante entender o que cada tecnologia oferece para escolher o equipamento que faz sentido para a sua necessidade”, explica Gilberto Gandelman, CEO da Proeletronic.

Com mais de 30 anos de atuação no mercado, a Proeletronic é uma empresa brasileira especializada no desenvolvimento e na fabricação de soluções para recepção e distribuição de sinais de TV aberta e paga, além de produtos para segurança, áudio e vídeo, telefonia e internet.

A companhia possui unidades industriais em Paraisópolis (MG) e Jacareí (SP) e atua em diferentes segmentos do setor eletroeletrônico, com portfólio que inclui soluções para TV, telefonia móvel, fechaduras, pilhas e baterias, sensores de presença, cabos, suportes para TV, além de produtos voltados a provedores de internet (ISPs) e infraestrutura de fibra óptica.

A linha de fibra óptica, comercializada sob a marca TERAPRO, atende provedores de internet em todo o país. Com presença em todo o território nacional por meio de uma ampla rede de distribuidores, varejistas, representantes e e-commerce, a Pro Eletronic também exporta seus produtos para a América Latina e a Europa.

A empresa é certificada ISO 9001 e possui certificação em conformidade com os requisitos da Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados (LGPD).

A atenção à experiência do consumidor também integra a atuação da Proeletronic, que em 2026 concorre ao Prêmio Reclame AQUI na categoria Eletrônicos – Fabricantes.

articles.body: Farrhana Bhatt, who emerged as one of the finalists of Khatron Ke Khiladi 15, has opened up about the physical challenges she faced while shooting for the stunt-based reality show in Cape Town. During an interaction with Hauterrfly on The Male Feminist episode, Farrhana recalled how the first stunt of the season turned into a frightening experience for her.Farrhana shared that her condition worsened after she returned to her hotel. Recalling the experience, she said, “After that I went to my hotel and I haven’t had cramps like that in my entire life. I could not even stand, I froze.” She added that she contacted her gynaecologist, who attributed the symptoms to stress and the sudden physical and emotional pressure her body had experienced.The actor also revealed that she was worried about how she would manage the next day’s stunt while dealing with such severe pain. According to Farrhana, this was the first time she had to rely on painkillers to get through the demanding schedule. She disclosed that she was taking two painkillers every day during that period.Farrhana further explained that the problem did not end with the shoot in South Africa. When she returned to India, she experienced the same bleeding again after three months. She consulted her doctor once more and was reportedly told that stress could be responsible for the symptoms.Speaking about how difficult the experience was, Farrhana said, “I can’t even explain the pain. I did not tell anyone about this, it is just my habit that even when something happens, I keep it to myself.” She also spoke about experiencing anxiety attacks while participating in Bigg Boss, revealing another aspect of the emotional challenges she has faced during reality television appearances.Farrhana Bhatt on taking a break from adventure-based reality showsIn September, Farrhana had spoken about wanting to step away from physically and emotionally challenging reality shows for some time after her experience on Khatron Ke Khiladi 15. She also clarified that she would not be joining the upcoming season of Roadies as a gang leader.More about Khatron Ke Khiladi 15Hosted by filmmaker Rohit Shetty, Khatron Ke Khiladi 15 returned to television after a two-year break. The season featured several popular television and entertainment personalities competing in challenging stunts involving heights, water, animals and other fear-based tasks.Avinash emerged as the winner of the season, while Rithvik Dhanjani and Orhan Awatramani, popularly known as Orry, secured the first and second runner-up positions, respectively.The contestant lineup included Rubina Dilaik, Jasmin Bhasin, Karan Wahi, Rithvik Dhanjani, Vishal Aditya Singh, Shagun Sharma, Avika Gor, Avinash Mishra, Harsh Gujral and Ruhaanika Dhawan, among others.Get the latest TV News, TV Shows and more. articles.title: Tesla is ‘winding down’ production of the Cybertruck next year
articles.summary: Tesla is getting the Cybertruck ready for retirement in an effort to ramp up its robotaxi output.﻿
articles.body: Tesla is getting the Cybertruck ready for retirement in an effort to ramp up its robotaxi output. In an X post on Friday, Tesla CEO Elon Musk said that the company will be “winding down” Cybertruck production at its Texas Gigafactory sometime around the middle of next year, “to make room for increased Cybercab production.” The production plant in Austin, Texas, is the only Tesla facility that’s known to assemble the Cybertruck, and that’s equipped to make the specialized components required to build the vehicles. Musk hasn’t mentioned if Cybertruck production will be moved elsewhere, but doing so would be arduous, especially for a car that’s never sold well. While Tesla doesn’t break out individual Cybertruck sales figures, even the highest analyst estimates place the total number of deliveries at roughly 70,000 since its launch in 2023 — significantly below the 250,000 that Musk once predicted would be sold annually. The Cybertruck has also been mired in controversy since it was introduced, from its divisive design (that isn’t road legal in many parts of the world), the numerous recalls for faulty or outright dangerous components, and the fatal accidents it’s been involved in. It’s an unusually long and complicated history for a vehicle that’s only been on the road for three years. If the Cybertruck does meet its demise in 2027, Tesla still has another ridiculous vehicle on the horizon to serve as its spiritual successor.

articles.title: The Enough Phone is made by and for people fed up with big screens
articles.summary: The Enough Phone is one startup’s attempt to revive the small form factor, offering iPhone Mini-ish dimensions and the option of a minimalist operating system.
articles.body: It’s a bad time and maybe also a great time to make a new smartphone. Brennan Jordan and Austin Boer are two-thirds of the trio behind the Enough Phone, a small phone that will run your choice of stock Android or the minimalist OdysseyOS. They’re currently seeking funding on Kickstarter, and just a day after launching, the project is over halfway to its $250,000 goal. The Enough Phone’s target specifications include a 5.3-inch display, 3,500mAh user-replaceable battery, MediaTek Dimensity 7500 chipset, a 50-megapixel Sony sensor in the rear camera, and 8GB of RAM. The dimensions listed on the Kickstarter page suggest an iPhone Mini-ish size; Jordan and Boer also happen to be former iPhone Mini users themselves. [Image: This prototype unit shows the user-removable back plate that will allow for simple battery swaps. The two of them cofounded a software startup called Sleke, which sells refurbished phones loaded with OdysseyOS, their minimalist, low-distraction version of Android. Putting the software on existing phones is a win for sustainability, but it also helps them get their software to market faster, Boer tells me. The pair offers small batches of Pixel 8 and 9 phones right now through the Sleke website, but the large devices didn’t feel quite right to some customers. “One of the biggest things that we get is, ‘I don’t want this large of a phone for a minimal operating system,’” says Boer. They’d wanted to make a small phone, and the opportunity arrived when Will Stults approached them about creating one. Stults operates an online store for non-smartphones called Dumbwireless. He also brings familiarity with the smartphone manufacturing process to the mix thanks to some previous work with a “big” phone brand. [Media: But hardware is hard in the best of times, and 2026 has proven extremely challenging for phone companies big and small. The chip shortage has driven prices up and made RAM scarce. Jordan and Boer are feeling the pressures, particularly around pricing. The Kickstarter campaign offers some discounts for early backers, but after that the Enough Phone will sell for $599. “We don’t want to be charging as much as we are,” says Boer, “but as a startup you can only do so much.” They’re a self-funded operation and want to keep it that way, he says, so they can choose their own priorities. Outside funding would change the dynamic and might put pressure on them to shorten their promised five years of software support or cut other costs. As it stands, the project is on schedule. According to the Kickstarter page, it’s in the production tooling phase, with plans to ship phones to customers in May 2027 — though a footnote says that the RAM shortage’s “ripple effects across the entire electronics manufacturing industry” could still throw a wrench in the works. Prospects for small phone fans (disclosure: I am one) were bleak even before the chip crisis. Apple’s last Mini was released five years ago, and there’s no indication of another one in sight. Asus’ Zenfone used to be a nice, small-ish Android option before the company made it bigger and quit selling it in the US. Pebble founder Eric Migicovsky made a lot of noise about launching a small phone, but has since shifted priorities. And there’s Unihertz’s Jelly Max — certainly small, but its specs lag behind a modern midrange phone. Boer sees this gap as an opportunity, even in the midst of a global RAM crisis. “Nobody was doing it, and we’re kind of seeing why — because it’s not the ideal time to start. But that also kind of makes it the ideal time to start, because no one else is doing it,” he says. “Let’s just do it ourselves.” Enough is enough. At least that’s what they’re hoping.

articles.title: After printing 40,000 whistles, this is the 3D printer I’d buy
articles.summary: The Verge reviews the $649 Bambu P2S 3D printer with its AMS 2 Pro multi-material system.
articles.body: I’ve been wanting to try 3D printing, people tell me. Which printer should I get? I finally have a fairly easy answer: the Bambu Lab P2S Combo. The auto-loading, fully enclosed touchscreen printer is one of the very few I can recommend. It’s the only one I’d buy for myself. It’s on sale for $649 through December 1st, but I’d vouch for it even at its normal $749 price. I’ve spent an entire year testing the P2S alongside several competitors, printing 40,000 whistles for ICE whistleblowers along the way. After racking up 6,770 hours of print time across four different printers, I’m sure of my recommendation. [Product: Bambu Lab P2S Combo | Some people who know 3D printers will argue with me: * Some will say you shouldn’t support Bambu because it’s profiting at the open-source community’s expense. * Others will say you shouldn’t spend so much when a $369 Elegoo Centauri Carbon 2 Combo or a $509 Bambu P1S Combo can print just as well. * Some will say you should save $100 or more by skipping multicolor “Combo” systems. * Some may even say, “What about all the fancy new tool-changing printers you just wrote about, Sean? Won’t the leaked P3C make the P2S obsolete?” But for the reasons I’ll explain below, the P2S Combo is my pick despite all of that. It’s durable, reliable, and simple to maintain and clean and forget about, even in ways my trusty Bambu P1P and the similar P1S lacked. The P2S makes 3D printing easy. When I’m in the mood, I don’t even need to walk over to my printer half the time. I can fire it up from my phone or laptop, using Bambu’s app to send one of millions of ready-made models from the cloud. The automated material system (AMS) automatically loads one of the rolls of filament that I leave in its protected enclosure for months at at time without fear. It automatically calibrates, automatically prints, automatically winds the filament back up when it’s done. [Image: I test and save one whistle from every batch I print, and it’s adding up! I tell friends that no matter which printer you buy, you should buy a multi-material system “Combo” because manually loading and unloading filament is a chore; it means standing around a printer waiting for it to heat up and feeding plastic into a tube by hand. Automated filament systems can fix that. For me, it’s not about having lots of colors in a single print; it’s about knowing I can print something black, or white, or red, or my kid’s favorite sparkly purple without any further effort — because I loaded those colors weeks ago. It is true that the $369 Elegoo Centauri Carbon 2 Combo also has automatic four-color filament feeding at a seemingly unbeatable price, and printed whistles and household items just as well as the P2S. I’ve spent 1,271 hours printing with the Centauri Carbon, and 939 hours with a Centauri Carbon 2, and they printed almost flawlessly right out of the box — no need to level a bed, no need to adjust belt tension, the printer calibrates itself. [Image: The Elegoo printed many beautiful whistles for me. But like other Bambu rivals, Elegoo doesn’t automatically load its filament from mostly airtight containers. I can’t leave rolls of filament in the printer for weeks or months when I’m not actively using them because they’ll quickly absorb moisture from the air, turn brittle, and jam up the printer’s tubes or nozzle. Moisture is the primary reason I wouldn’t recommend an inexpensive Bambu A1 Combo to newcomers, either, or a Snapmaker U1, or any other attractive multicolor printer without sealed filament storage. The entire experience of using a 3D printer is friendlier when you don’t have to prep the printer before printing. [Image: Like most printers, Elegoo stores its filament on the outside, which doesn’t protect against moisture. Also, I found certain kinds of spools can slip off the spindles — even if they’re made by Elegoo! Bambu’s AMS, meanwhile, can have issues with lightweight cardboard spools. Even so, it’s pretty dang tempting to save $280 or more by going with the Elegoo. But over the course of the roughly 1,000 hours I tested the Carbon and Carbon 2 side by side with the Bambu P2S, the Elegoo printers broke down in ways that were more difficult to diagnose. The original Carbon’s extruder had some feeding issues and I found a lot of black dust inside after taking it apart, seemingly from worn plastic gears. Just this week, my Carbon 2’s stopped working after its nozzle mysteriously crashed into the bed and it refused to auto-level itself (which would normally fix that issue). I had to take the bed apart and still couldn’t find anything wrong. In the end, yanking and reseating four tiny fragile-and-yet-too-tight connectors inside the bed fixed that problem, but it’s not the kind of solution a consumer should have to do. [Image: Apologies for the slightly blurry photo; I was holding the heatbed cover with my other hand. Anecdotally, my Bambu printers have led a comparatively charmed life: In 1,692 hours of printing with the P2S, I’ve had to swap out the nozzle twice, clean and relubricate the traversal rods and screws several times, wash the removable magnetic printing surfaces a bunch of times with water and dish soap, and clear several filament jams in the AMS. That’s about it. P2S nozzle replacements are easier, too. When you jam today’s Elegoo printers, you’re going old-school, either by wrenching off a hot nozzle so you can clean or inexpensively replace it ($25 for eight nozzles) or by fishing out tiny wires and unscrewing two bolts to remove an entire $30 hotend (which includes the elements that heat the plastic) at once. With Bambu’s P2S, you can just yank off a gasket and open one spring clip to swap a whole new toolless hotend ($18) in less than a minute. It does help to have a pair of mini pliers to grab the nozzle, though. [Image: My P2S review unit, humming away at printing whistles. The Elegoo printers also have noisy fans that stay active even when you’re not printing, unlike the Bambu, though the Centauri Carbon 2 does shut them off more quickly than the original. Both Elegoo and Bambu let you remotely monitor your prints from its built-in camera and capture timelapse videos, but Elegoo’s camera and lighting are crap quality by comparison. If I’m being completely honest, Bambu’s own Bambu P1S Combo, at $509 on sale, is the closest competition for the $649 P2S Combo, and I had a hunch it might be my pick in the end. I upgraded my P1P with most of the P1S upgrades, and it’s been a reliable workhorse: nearly 3,000 hours of 3D printing so far. [Image: Time sure does fly by. In fact, it’ll be at 2,870 hours by the time you read this story. But over the past year, I’ve gravitated towards the P2S more and more because of its easy-swap hotends, the built-in touchscreen where I easily manage prints and rolls of filament, and all kinds of little improvements that I find I actually care about: * It has a built-in guide that helps me put the P2S’s magnetic build plate in the right place every time, saving me from failures I’ve had with the P1P. * It’ll automatically detect if I forget to put the build plate back, too, which saved me once this past year. * The nozzle wiper is better at removing ooze that might wind up in your print and the poop chute clogs less. * You don’t need to leave the door or lid open when printing PLA because it has active ventilation. * It’s easier to add a second AMS later for four more colors, or just a single fifth roll on an external spindle. * The stainless steel linear rods are easier to clean. * I can sweep debris right out of the enclosure because the floor is a smooth ramp. * The camera’s better, and video from it is far better lit. * The AMS 2 makes it far easier to clear bits of old brittle filament without taking the unit apart. Plus, I did have to replace the entire heatbed on my P1P once. I can’t say that nothing will go wrong with the P2S, and you shouldn’t take away that they’re as simple as an inkjet. They will need occasional maintenance, you’ll need to load good-quality filament and probably want to avoid rolls that come on lightweight cardboard (I try to buy Bambu, Sunlu, or Elegoo refills for my reusable plastic Bambu spools), and even then there will be components that wear out. [Image: Even with care, an AMS can occasionally tie a roll of filament in a knot if one coil slips under another. This one was easy to fix. After 1,600 hours, the AMS 2 that came with my Bambu P2S review unit sometimes complains when trying to unwind or rewind some rolls of filament from some slots, and I suspect it’s because some of the gears are wearing prematurely. Bambu recently announced it’ll replace some of those gears free of charge, but only ones manufactured between May and July 2026, and even then you’ll have to be pretty handy to install them yourself. [Media: I strongly believe people buying their first printer should get something tried and true, fully baked, simple to use, and the P2S is the best yet. But even Bambu is still catering more to DIY enthusiasts who’ll tolerate the occasional hardware defect. So yes, if you’re asking “Which printer should I get,” I think you’d be pleasantly surprised with a P2S! But I wouldn’t blame you for waiting a few more years.

articles.title: I’ve reviewed almost every Android foldable this year — here’s how the iPhone Duo compares
articles.summary: Apple’s first foldable matches its Android rivals in a few key areas, but it falls short in others.
articles.body: When I first read Allison and Nilay’s Verge review of the iPhone Duo, I was immediately struck by one of their complaints: that the cover display is too small. That’s not how the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 feels, I thought. Had they got it wrong? After a week and a half using the Duo, I know exactly what they mean — and it’s not the screen’s fault at all. Apps that feel comfortable on Samsung’s short foldable and the similarly sized Xiaomi 18 Fold are often cramped and compact on the Duo’s cover screen, robbed of screen space by a right-hand rail that most apps don’t make use of anyway. That’s just one of the ways that Apple’s first foldable feels fundamentally different from the Android alternatives. I’ve reviewed almost every Android foldable that was released this year, from Samsung and Google to Honor and Oppo, and I’ve been surprised to realize that the Duo holds its own against them all on hardware, but is let down by iOS itself. For now at least, Android is slicker for folding phones — though I don’t know how long that will last. Size, shape, and build quality The iPhone Duo feels great. Mostly. Its curved frame and Ceramic Shield back have that ineffable Apple feeling, a sense of polish that helps justify the $2,000 price tag. The hinge in particular is satisfyingly smooth, closing and opening with a comforting magnetic click. Compared with the Galaxy Z Fold 8 or Xiaomi 18 Fold, the Duo just feels better. But part of that is down to the Duo’s big drawback: its weight. At first it feels encouraging, the reassuring heft of all that glass and metal. Then I started using the phone, and I realized it’s just plain heavy. It weighs more than all of its rivals — even ones with larger screens — and any attempt to use the Duo one-handed makes that obvious quickly. It’s a little thicker than some other foldables, too, though in practice that bothers me far less. [Image: Honor’s Magic V6 (right) is the thinnest foldable around, but not by enough to really matter. The squat shape won’t be for everyone. The Duo is even shorter and wider than the Z Fold 8, though almost identical in dimensions to Xiaomi’s 18 Fold. I’m a fan of this design, which is both cute and comfortable when folded shut and gives you a natural choice of portrait or landscape orientations when open. The major downsides are that the short cover screen makes some apps awkward to use, and it’s wide when you need to stretch across to the other side — a problem worsened by some of Apple’s software choices. More on that later. And while the Duo’s IP68 rating is an obvious advantage over much of the competition (only Google and Honor can match it), we’ve not seen many recent Android foldables struggle with hinge and display damage quite like the Duo. It’s still not clear how widespread Duo screen failures really are — they don’t seem to be as ubiquitous as Samsung’s first-generation failures back in 2019 — but non-impact damage like this is almost unheard of in modern Android foldables. It’s a reminder that the Duo is still a first-gen product while some Android rivals are into their eighth iteration. The crease and screen The screen is the Duo’s smartest hardware trick, and easily my favorite thing about the phone compared with other foldable phones. No rival offers anything like the “nano-texture” (read: matte) finish on the inner screen, which is easy on the eyes in more ways than one. [Image: The Duo’s crease (right) is about as hard to spot as the Oppo Find N6’s. Crucially, it also helps mask the phone’s crease, which isn’t quite invisible but is well-hidden. The Duo’s crease is somewhere in the middle of the Android pack: subtler than Google’s and Honor’s, more obvious than Samsung’s. Oppo’s near-invisible crease remains the best, but not by much. The Duo’s matte screen means it’s harder than most to see (though visible from an angle), but it’s still easy enough to feel, and a couple of friends have immediately remarked on it when trying the phone. Still, I don’t want to over-egg it: The Pixel 11 Pro Fold is probably the only one out of this year’s foldables with a crease I’d say is a problem. The Duo’s crease is easy to ignore. I’d actually say the Duo’s under-display camera is more of an annoyance. It’s not only inside an extra-pixelated circle of screen, but that’s the only patch without the matte coating, which makes it a little more distracting. I can mostly tune it out, but not entirely. I’d probably prefer a regular selfie camera tucked right into the corner, as on the Xiaomi 18 Fold and a few others, but I suspect opinions will differ here. Finally, the Duo benefits from stylus support, letting you use a USB-C Apple Pencil on the central screen. This isn’t unique — Samsung used to offer the same, and both of Honor’s and Oppo’s latest foldables work with their styli — but plenty of the current Android crop don’t offer the option. I don’t have an Apple Pencil, so I haven’t been able to test it myself, but my colleague Allison is clearly a fan. Cameras and battery life [Image: Despite being the same size, Xiaomi’s 18 Fold (right) fits in a triple rear camera. The iPhone Duo’s cameras, like those on most foldables, are fairly basic, with a pair of 48-megapixel rear lenses, one main and one ultrawide. It’s a setup comparable to the Z Fold 8, and both phones’ cameras are good, but not great. Most other Android foldables (including Samsung’s Z Fold 8 Ultra) instead offer triple rear cameras, netting you a big boost in photographic flexibility. They often use larger sensors than either Apple or Samsung, so their main cameras are better, too. Still, Vivo is the only manufacturer getting close to slab flagship quality in its foldable cameras, and its hardware lags behind in a few other respects that would prevent it from being my foldable recommendation overall. As for selfies, the front-screen camera is pretty basic, but you can take better shots using the rear cameras by opening the phone up and flipping it round. That under-display camera is worse than a regular selfie camera, but good enough so long as you only use it for video calls. As for battery, Nilay and Allison had different experiences in our Duo review. I’ve mostly found the battery long-lasting, easily running a full day of mixed use. It’s got a higher capacity than either of Samsung’s foldables, so that’s no real surprise. It still pales in comparison to the two-day battery of Honor’s Magic V6, but once you’re past lasting a day, I think you get diminishing returns anyway. Software support and multitasking [Image: On hardware alone, the Duo holds its own. So far, the Duo looks like a competitive foldable, albeit a little middle-of-the-pack. It beats its rivals in some hardware areas, falls behind in others, and has one truly unique selling point in the matte foldable display. Unusually for Apple, the software is what lets it down. The biggest problem isn’t Apple’s own software, but everyone else’s: Most apps still aren’t optimized for the Duo. In the best case, that means apps that don’t make full use of the Duo’s new right-hand rail, showing an empty black bar instead of app controls. Worse are the ones that don’t even scale to the larger screen — apps like Bluesky or Duolingo can use the whole display on other foldables, but appear in thin strips with huge black bars on the Duo. This will improve with time. I’ve seen Google Maps, Google Translate, and Instagram update in the last few days alone, and no doubt more will follow. Some are already better on the Duo: Slack uses a helpful desktop-style two-column layout, while on Android foldables you just get the mobile UI but bigger. But for now at least, most apps run better on my Android foldables than on my Duo. [Image: The Xiaomi 18 Fold (right) makes full use of its cover screen, though different app scaling can affect how useful that is. OS-level improvements are harder to predict. At first I loved the idea of Apple moving key controls to the right-hand edge, but it takes up so much space that it leaves the Duo’s cover screen feeling smaller than it needs to: You get all the awkward stretching of a wide phone without the expansive screen space. Samsung and Xiaomi’s wide foldables may be about the same size, but in use they feel much bigger. I wonder how many software developers will follow Google’s lead in app optimization — it essentially ignored the right rail entirely while updating Google Maps, instead just spreading the map to the edge of the screen. It feels bigger and better than most other Duo apps as a result. And this is partly the Android user in me, but the lack of a persistent back-swipe gesture seems to grate more on the Duo than on other iPhones. Sometimes, moving backward in an app requires a button in the right rail, sometimes one in the top-left corner, sometimes a swipe from the left-hand edge of the screen. It’s annoyingly inconsistent, and more often than not requires stretching across the phone’s width, whether it’s open or closed. Being able to swipe back from either side of the screen gives Android foldables a huge advantage in one-handed use. [Image: Xiaomi’s 18 Fold (right) has substantially more flexible multitasking than the Duo. As for multitasking, the Duo is well behind the competition. You can run two apps at once in split-screen, but only in landscape mode, and each must take up exactly half the display. Compare this to Oppo, which allows you to fluidly move between multiple split-screen apps and floating windows; or Xiaomi, which allows up to six apps to run side by side in split-screen, and Apple’s implementation feels downright basic. These are the extreme end of Android, and probably overkill for most (they certainly are for me), but I’d take them over Apple’s half-hearted multitasking any day. The bottom line Apple hasn’t waded into the foldable market and fixed all its flaws. If anything, “crackgate” is proof that it’s still playing catch-up with the Android alternatives, which have a few years of fine-tuning behind them. Many are still lighter, and thinner, and have subtler creases than the Duo, or bigger batteries and better cameras. In broad strokes, though, this hardware is up to scratch — and, crucially, on par with its most direct worldwide rival, the Galaxy Z Fold 8. For now, though, Android has the software edge. Google has worked hard to make its OS adaptable to various screen sizes so most apps take full advantage of the bigger inner screen while individual OEMs have designed ambitious multitasking tools. That isn’t yet true for iOS, and some of Apple’s own software tweaks in the OS make things more awkward still. It’s those that I’m worried about long term. The best thing about foldables is their flexibility — something Apple itself often lacks. If the Duo is going to catch up to Android, Apple might have to adapt. articles.title: Your old Android phone could become a walking robot
articles.summary: UCLA's PhoneBot turns old Android phones into the brain of a two-legged humanoid robot that walks, follows people and stands up after falling.
articles.body: Got an old Android phone collecting dust in a drawer? You might want to hang on to it. Researchers at UCLA have figured out how to turn an aging smartphone into the brain of a small walking robot. It's called PhoneBot, and it can walk on two legs, follow people and even get back up after falling face down. The most surprising part? The researchers estimate the robot's hardware costs about $400, excluding the phone. So, that forgotten smartphone could have a pretty interesting second life. Here's how the researchers pulled it off and what it would take to build one yourself. Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money. Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com. GOOGLE TURNS OLD PHONES INTO CLOUD SERVERS How UCLA turned an old Android phone into a walking robot PhoneBot comes from UCLA's Robotics and Mechanisms Laboratory, also known as RoMeLa. The team built a miniature humanoid robot that stands about 19 inches tall and weighs roughly four pounds, including the smartphone attached to its body. Instead of developing an expensive custom computer, researchers used technology already inside an Android phone. The robot has 13 motorized joints, with six in each leg and another that lets its upper body rotate. That extra movement allows the smartphone's camera to turn toward someone while the robot's feet stay planted. The researchers’ goal is to make humanoid robotics more affordable for schools and research teams that cannot spend thousands of dollars on specialized machines. Your old Android phone becomes the robot's brain Think about everything your smartphone already does. It can recognize objects through its camera and detect movement using built-in sensors. It also has enough processing power to run sophisticated software. PhoneBot puts those capabilities to work. An Android app uses the phone's motion sensors to help the robot maintain its balance. Meanwhile, the camera helps it recognize and track people. The phone also runs an artificial intelligence-powered walking controller that tells the robot how to move. Those instructions travel over Wi-Fi to a small computer inside the robot, which communicates with the motors. The smartphone has no physical electrical connection to the robot's hardware. That design makes it easier to swap phones without rewiring the machine. Researchers trained PhoneBot's walking system in computer simulations before testing it on the actual robot. They also developed a way to improve how evenly it uses both legs. As a result, PhoneBot can walk on flat surfaces and stand up from a face-down position. For something powered largely by an old smartphone, that's quite an accomplishment. Even a nearly 10-year-old Android phone can work Here's something I found especially interesting. UCLA didn't need the latest expensive smartphone to make PhoneBot work. In fact, the researchers successfully tested its core functions on four different Android devices, including an Honor 9 released back in 2017. The other models included a Samsung Galaxy A16 5G and two Motorola Moto G phones from 2024 and 2025. Researchers purchased the three prepaid models for roughly $50 to $90 each. Those were the prices reported during testing, rather than guaranteed prices today. All four phones handled the essential functions, including movement control and camera-based recognition. However, the older Honor 9 could not run one of the robot's mapping features because the required Google services were unavailable on that device in the United States. That means you cannot assume every Android phone will work. Still, the tests suggest you may not need an expensive new phone to run a capable little robot. A WHEELED ROBOT MAY BEAT HUMANOIDS INTO YOUR HOME Can PhoneBot follow you around? Yes, at least within the limits of what UCLA has demonstrated. PhoneBot can use its smartphone camera to identify a person and adjust its movement to follow them. It can also rotate its upper body to keep someone in view. The robot supports conversational interaction, too. However, there's an important limitation. Its current system uses a separate laptop to process speech and generate AI responses. The smartphone records your voice and plays the response through its speaker. Before you start thinking about having PhoneBot clean your house, there's something else you should know. It doesn't have arms. That means it cannot pick up your laundry or carry groceries. Researchers also trained its walking system on flat ground, so navigating stairs and uneven surfaces remains a challenge. For now, PhoneBot is best viewed as an experimental platform. UCLA has demonstrated what it can do under research conditions, but it hasn't established that the robot can independently navigate a typical home. Could you build a walking robot with your own Android phone? If you're comfortable with electronics and robotics, PhoneBot could become a pretty interesting project. UCLA has developed it as an open-source research platform and published hardware designs and building resources. The official PhoneBot website at phonebot.dev/ provides information about the robot's design, components and assembly process. The published hardware materials are available for noncommercial use under a Creative Commons license. There's an important distinction, though, between having the hardware plans and being able to build a fully working robot. The project website provides hardware designs and assembly resources but does not clearly offer a download for the complete Android app and trained walking software. Although UCLA describes PhoneBot as an open-source platform, anyone hoping to reproduce its capabilities should first confirm that the necessary software is available. And there's another consideration: the $400 price tag. It's an approximate hardware cost, and it doesn't include the smartphone. Depending on what equipment you already have, you may also need access to a 3D printer and tools for assembly. Shipping and other expenses could push the total higher. You'll also need the technical skills to put everything together and configure the software. So, don't expect to download an app and watch your old phone suddenly sprout legs. There's real engineering involved. Why PhoneBot could make walking robots more affordable Humanoid robots are getting a lot of attention, but building one remains expensive. Some small research models cost several thousand dollars. More advanced systems can cost considerably more. PhoneBot takes advantage of hardware that millions of people already own. By letting a smartphone handle much of the sensing and computing, researchers can avoid buying some specialized components. That helps bring the overall cost down. The approach could also make robotics more accessible to students. Instead of requiring a large research budget, a smaller team could experiment with a relatively inexpensive walking machine. They could test new software or explore ways to improve movement without building every electronic component from scratch. The UCLA team already has ideas for what comes next. Researchers want to improve PhoneBot's ability to handle uneven terrain and eventually give it lightweight arms. They're also exploring ways to run more conversational AI directly on the smartphone, which could reduce the need for a separate computer. Those improvements are still future goals. Even so, PhoneBot offers a promising starting point for building more affordable humanoid robots. What this means to you You probably won't see PhoneBot on store shelves anytime soon. But this research shows how much useful technology may still be inside a smartphone you've stopped using. A phone that feels outdated for daily use could still handle surprisingly demanding tasks. If you're interested in robotics, PhoneBot could eventually offer a more affordable way to experiment with walking machines. Meanwhile, for families with kids who love technology, an accessible version of this project could make for a fascinating hands-on learning experience. And if you've been thinking about getting rid of your old Android phone, this research offers another reason to consider what it might still be capable of. Of course, building a robot won't be for everyone. You can also sell, donate or recycle your old phone. Before you do, check out our article on securely getting rid of your old cell phone to make sure your personal information doesn't go along with it. Kurt's key takeaways I love the idea that a smartphone sitting forgotten in a drawer could become the brain of a walking robot. We've gotten so used to replacing our phones every few years that we sometimes overlook how powerful these devices still are. What UCLA has done with PhoneBot makes me wonder how many other uses we're missing. Now, let's be realistic. This little guy isn't ready to take over household chores, and putting one together requires some serious know-how. But the price is what caught my attention. When researchers can build a walking robot with roughly $400 in additional hardware, it opens the door to possibilities that once seemed out of reach. I'd love to see someone turn this into an affordable kit that families could build together. That could be a great way to get kids excited about engineering. Would you spend a few hundred dollars to turn your old Android phone into a walking robot? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com. articles.title: Apple has a secret list of banned autocomplete phrases including ‘dictator Trump’ and ‘covid is a hoax’
articles.summary: A researcher found a list of over 100,000 words in phrases in multiple languages Apple blocks from autocomplete and swipe-type suggestions in iOS.
articles.body: A researcher found over 100,000 words and phrases in “every major language” that are blocked from autocomplete and swipe-type in iOS, Reuters reports. The researcher, Derik Kauffman, says you can still type the words on the blocklist one letter at a time. But they won’t pop up as predictive text suggestions and iOS’s keyboard may automatically alter them when swipe-typing, like changing “left wing conspiracy” to “left wrong conspiracy.” Kauffman posted the full list online, including the individual lists for different languages. Most of the words and phrases on the list are offensive, slurs, or related to topics like sex and drugs. But it also contains political phrases like “illegal immigrant,” “dictator Trump,” “sleepy Joe,” “covid was a hoax,” and “left wing conspiracy” as well as some less controversial phrases like “Santa isn’t real” and “iMessage isn’t working.” Kauffman found some discrepancies on the list, too, where one phrase is blocked while its counterpart isn’t, such as blocking “bad girl” but not “bad boy.” According to Reuters, Kauffman used OpenAI’s Codex and Anthropic’s Claude Code to help find the list “deep in the bowels” of iOS. On his website, Kauffman says the phrase list was stored as a hash table, which he was able to convert back to text. Another researcher told Reuters they were able to independently obtain the same list. Apple told Reuters that its keyboard is designed to avoid potentially inappropriate or offensive suggestions, but iPhone users can still type in what they want, or override predictive text suggestions. “Apple did not immediately respond to The Verge’s request for comment.
